subject: Accounting
title: Mixed Costs
description: A fast breakdown of Mixed Costs for builders.

hook.text: Your phone plan costs $30/month plus $0.10 per extra minute. Fixed and variable combined.

buildup.text: Mixed costs have both a fixed component and a variable component that changes with activity.

discovery.text: Utilities are classic mixed costs—a base charge plus usage fees that rise with consumption.

twist.text: Separating the fixed and variable parts of mixed costs is essential for accurate analysis.

climax.text: The high-low method and regression analysis help accountants split mixed costs into their parts.

punchline.text: Some costs are fixed. Some are variable. Some are both.

quiz.question: What is a mixed cost?
options: A cost with both fixed and variable components
A cost that only occurs occasionally
A cost shared between two departments

details.summary: Mixed costs contain both a fixed component and a variable component—like a utility bill with a base charge plus a per-unit usage fee. This topic explains how to separate the fixed and variable portions using methods like the high-low method and regression analysis.
details.whyItMatters: Budgeting and break-even analysis require costs to be classified as fixed or variable. Mixed costs must be split into their components before they can be used in these calculations.
takeaways: Mixed costs have a base fixed amount plus a variable amount that changes with activity
The high-low method uses the highest and lowest activity points to estimate cost behavior
Regression analysis uses all data points for a more statistically reliable cost estimate

faq.question: What is a mixed cost?
faq.answer: A mixed cost has both fixed and variable components. For example, a phone bill might have a $50 monthly base fee (fixed) plus $0.10 per minute of usage (variable). The total cost changes with activity but never drops to zero because of the fixed portion.

faq.question: How does the high-low method separate mixed costs?
faq.answer: Take the highest and lowest activity levels and their corresponding total costs. The variable cost per unit equals the difference in costs divided by the difference in activity. The fixed cost equals the total cost at either point minus the variable portion.
